evidence.claim: Oatman’s fortunes followed gold first and highway traffic later.
evidence.quote: Oatman was fortunate it was located on busy U.S. Route 66 and catered to travelers driving between Kingman, Arizona, and Needles, California.

evidence.claim: The opening of the Tom Reed mine and a 1915 discovery at United Eastern brought a gold rush to the Black Mountains.
evidence.quote: The opening of the Tom Reed mine, followed by the discovery of a rich ore body in the nearby United Eastern Mining Company's property in 1915, brought one of the desert's last gold rushes.

evidence.claim: United Eastern stopped operating in 1924.
evidence.quote: In 1924, the town's main employer, United Eastern Mines, permanently shut down its operations

evidence.claim: The town then served Route 66 travelers between Kingman and Needles, until a new alignment bypassed it.
evidence.quote: the town was completely bypassed in 1953 when a new route was built between Kingman and Needles.

evidence.claim: By the 1960s it was almost abandoned.
evidence.quote: By the 1960s, Oatman was all but abandoned.

evidence.claim: Its present Route 66 identity includes wooden sidewalks and wild burros wandering the streets.
evidence.quote: The town survives as a nostalgic Route 66 stop with a Wild West feel down to the wooden sidewalks, staged shootouts, and wild burros wandering the streets.
